case_info.scenario: A 50-year-old man was referred for ophthalmoplegia that developed immediately after an 8.5-hour robotic cystectomy for small cell cancer of the bladder. After recovering from anesthesia in the postanesthesia care unit, he experienced headache, facial numbness, inability to open both his eyes, and inability to move both eyes in any direction. He had a known enhancing central skull base lesion in sella turcica with compression of the optic chiasm and mild mass effect on the pons that was felt to be a pituitary macroadenoma (Figure). His baseline examination before the cystectomy showed visual acuity of 20/20 OU with intact extraocular movements and unremarkable confrontational fields, although a mild bitemporal hemianopia was seen on automated visual fields. During the bedside examination in the postanesthesia care unit, he was noted to have complete bilateral ptosis. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU with full visual fields on confrontational visual field testing. He had decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve bilaterally. The right and left pupils were 5 mm and 6 mm in size, respectively, in both light and dark. There was no pupillary response to light or accommodation. No exophthalmos was noted. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes. The patient was unable to move either eye in any direction on extraocular motility testing. Vestibulo-ocular reflex did not overcome the ophthalmoplegia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained 12 hours after symptom onset redemonstrating the large sellar mass, which no longer had central enhancement (Figure).
case_info.caption: T1-weighted coronal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast shows a 4.9 × 4.6 × 5.2-cm sellar/parasellar lobulated mass with homogenous enhancement before symptom onset (A), which became 5.3 × 5.1 × 5.3 cm and had loss of enhancement after symptom onset (B). The mass caused superior displacement of the optic chiasm and had extension into the cavernous sinus bilaterally. The mass also extended posteriorly and deformed the anterior aspect of the pons (not shown). After symptom onset, the mass was hyperintense on T2-weighted images (not shown).
case_info.explanation: Based on the acute presentation of symptoms and signs starting immediately after surgery and change in the appearance of tumor on MRI (loss of central enhancement), a diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy was made. The ophthalmoplegia in ocular motor apraxia can be overcome with vestibular ocular reflex, which was not the case here. The absence of exophthalmos and normal intraocular pressure argue against the diagnosis of orbital compartment syndrome. Imaging does not support the diagnosis of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pituitary apoplexy is an acute-onset syndrome due to hemorrhaging and/or infarction of the pituitary gland. Postoperative pituitary apoplexy has been reported after cardiac surgery, abdominal surgery, thyroidectomy, laparoscopic lumbar spinal fusion, and knee arthroplasty.1Risk factors proposed during surgery that could lead to pituitary apoplexy include prolonged mechanical ventilation, embolization, unstable blood pressure, anticoagulation, crystalloid hemodilution, previous treatment with dopamine agonists, and radiotherapy.2 Patients with pituitary apoplexy typically present with headaches. Cranial nerve palsies leading to ophthalmoplegia have been reported in about 50% of patients during pituitary apoplexy.1Sixty-four percent of patients can have vision loss from worsening chiasmal compression, which fortunately this patient did not have.3Early neuroimaging study is important to confirm the suspicion of pituitary apoplexy, along with urgent pituitary function tests. Computed tomography scan is often the first study performed in an acute setting and may demonstrate a variably hyperdense mass of the sella and suprasellar region in the presence of hemorrhage. MRI is the preferred study of choice with sensitivity of about 90%.4Appearance of hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy on MRI depends on the sequence and stage of hemorrhage. In the acute phase, hemorrhage is usually hypotense on T2-weighted imaging because of the presence of deoxyhemoglobin, which was not present in the present patient. Infarctive pituitary apoplexy alone, which is a rarer presentation of pituitary apoplexy, has low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and no contrast enhancement of the tumor as seen in this patient. It may have associated rim enhancement.5 Pituitary apoplexy is a vision- and life-threatening neuro-ophthalmic emergency. Before the use of corticosteroids, mortality rates were reported to be as high as 50% because of acute adrenal insufficiency that many of these patients develop. Treatment involves urgent administration of steroids, endocrine evaluation, and urgent surgical intervention for prompt decompression based on severity of presentation. Visual recovery, with or without sequelae, is variable depending on the severity and duration of compression of the optic nerve apparatus. Ophthalmoplegia resolves in the majority of patients, but some patients can have incomplete recovery.6,7 The patient immediately started receiving intravenous corticosteroids under the guidance of endocrinology and neurosurgery. He was monitored for any endocrine deficiencies while inpatient. After no improvement in extraocular movements were noted over 5 days, the patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of pituitary tumor. Pathological evaluation of the tumor confirmed a pituitary adenoma with areas of necrosis consistent with pituitary apoplexy. Postoperative MRI showed successful resection of the large pituitary macroadenoma, with decompression of the optic chiasm. There was some residual tumor in the bilateral cavernous sinuses, basisphenoid, and along the dorsum sella. One year after surgery, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal color vision. Bilateral ptosis had resolved. Extraocular movements were full and the eyes were well aligned. However, the pupils remained unresponsive to light and accommodation. The mild bitemporal hemianopsia remained unchanged from baseline on automated visual fields.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Based on the acute presentation of symptoms and signs starting immediately after surgery and change in the appearance of tumor on MRI (loss of central enhancement), a diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy was made. The ophthalmoplegia in ocular motor apraxia can be overcome with vestibular ocular reflex, which was not the case here. The absence of exophthalmos and normal intraocular pressure argue against the diagnosis of orbital compartment syndrome. Imaging does not support the diagnosis of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pituitary apoplexy is an acute-onset syndrome due to hemorrhaging and/or infarction of the pituitary gland. Postoperative pituitary apoplexy has been reported after cardiac surgery, abdominal surgery, thyroidectomy, laparoscopic lumbar spinal fusion, and knee arthroplasty.1Risk factors proposed during surgery that could lead to pituitary apoplexy include prolonged mechanical ventilation, embolization, unstable blood pressure, anticoagulation, crystalloid hemodilution, previous treatment with dopamine agonists, and radiotherapy.2 Patients with pituitary apoplexy typically present with headaches. Cranial nerve palsies leading to ophthalmoplegia have been reported in about 50% of patients during pituitary apoplexy.1Sixty-four percent of patients can have vision loss from worsening chiasmal compression, which fortunately this patient did not have.3Early neuroimaging study is important to confirm the suspicion of pituitary apoplexy, along with urgent pituitary function tests. Computed tomography scan is often the first study performed in an acute setting and may demonstrate a variably hyperdense mass of the sella and suprasellar region in the presence of hemorrhage. MRI is the preferred study of choice with sensitivity of about 90%.4Appearance of hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy on MRI depends on the sequence and stage of hemorrhage. In the acute phase, hemorrhage is usually hypotense on T2-weighted imaging because of the presence of deoxyhemoglobin, which was not present in the present patient. Infarctive pituitary apoplexy alone, which is a rarer presentation of pituitary apoplexy, has low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and no contrast enhancement of the tumor as seen in this patient. It may have associated rim enhancement.5 Pituitary apoplexy is a vision- and life-threatening neuro-ophthalmic emergency. Before the use of corticosteroids, mortality rates were reported to be as high as 50% because of acute adrenal insufficiency that many of these patients develop. Treatment involves urgent administration of steroids, endocrine evaluation, and urgent surgical intervention for prompt decompression based on severity of presentation. Visual recovery, with or without sequelae, is variable depending on the severity and duration of compression of the optic nerve apparatus. Ophthalmoplegia resolves in the majority of patients, but some patients can have incomplete recovery.6,7 The patient immediately started receiving intravenous corticosteroids under the guidance of endocrinology and neurosurgery. He was monitored for any endocrine deficiencies while inpatient. After no improvement in extraocular movements were noted over 5 days, the patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of pituitary tumor. Pathological evaluation of the tumor confirmed a pituitary adenoma with areas of necrosis consistent with pituitary apoplexy. Postoperative MRI showed successful resection of the large pituitary macroadenoma, with decompression of the optic chiasm. There was some residual tumor in the bilateral cavernous sinuses, basisphenoid, and along the dorsum sella. One year after surgery, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal color vision. Bilateral ptosis had resolved. Extraocular movements were full and the eyes were well aligned. However, the pupils remained unresponsive to light and accommodation. The mild bitemporal hemianopsia remained unchanged from baseline on automated visual fields.

next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.

[Cognitive Burden]

- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.

  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 2.2. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is

  score low.)

  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

case_info.explanation: Based on the acute presentation of symptoms and signs starting immediately after surgery and change in the appearance of tumor on MRI (loss of central enhancement), a diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy was made. The ophthalmoplegia in ocular motor apraxia can be overcome with vestibular ocular reflex, which was not the case here. The absence of exophthalmos and normal intraocular pressure argue against the diagnosis of orbital compartment syndrome. Imaging does not support the diagnosis of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pituitary apoplexy is an acute-onset syndrome due to hemorrhaging and/or infarction of the pituitary gland. Postoperative pituitary apoplexy has been reported after cardiac surgery, abdominal surgery, thyroidectomy, laparoscopic lumbar spinal fusion, and knee arthroplasty.1Risk factors proposed during surgery that could lead to pituitary apoplexy include prolonged mechanical ventilation, embolization, unstable blood pressure, anticoagulation, crystalloid hemodilution, previous treatment with dopamine agonists, and radiotherapy.2 Patients with pituitary apoplexy typically present with headaches. Cranial nerve palsies leading to ophthalmoplegia have been reported in about 50% of patients during pituitary apoplexy.1Sixty-four percent of patients can have vision loss from worsening chiasmal compression, which fortunately this patient did not have.3Early neuroimaging study is important to confirm the suspicion of pituitary apoplexy, along with urgent pituitary function tests. Computed tomography scan is often the first study performed in an acute setting and may demonstrate a variably hyperdense mass of the sella and suprasellar region in the presence of hemorrhage. MRI is the preferred study of choice with sensitivity of about 90%.4Appearance of hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy on MRI depends on the sequence and stage of hemorrhage. In the acute phase, hemorrhage is usually hypotense on T2-weighted imaging because of the presence of deoxyhemoglobin, which was not present in the present patient. Infarctive pituitary apoplexy alone, which is a rarer presentation of pituitary apoplexy, has low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and no contrast enhancement of the tumor as seen in this patient. It may have associated rim enhancement.5 Pituitary apoplexy is a vision- and life-threatening neuro-ophthalmic emergency. Before the use of corticosteroids, mortality rates were reported to be as high as 50% because of acute adrenal insufficiency that many of these patients develop. Treatment involves urgent administration of steroids, endocrine evaluation, and urgent surgical intervention for prompt decompression based on severity of presentation. Visual recovery, with or without sequelae, is variable depending on the severity and duration of compression of the optic nerve apparatus. Ophthalmoplegia resolves in the majority of patients, but some patients can have incomplete recovery.6,7 The patient immediately started receiving intravenous corticosteroids under the guidance of endocrinology and neurosurgery. He was monitored for any endocrine deficiencies while inpatient. After no improvement in extraocular movements were noted over 5 days, the patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of pituitary tumor. Pathological evaluation of the tumor confirmed a pituitary adenoma with areas of necrosis consistent with pituitary apoplexy. Postoperative MRI showed successful resection of the large pituitary macroadenoma, with decompression of the optic chiasm. There was some residual tumor in the bilateral cavernous sinuses, basisphenoid, and along the dorsum sella. One year after surgery, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal color vision. Bilateral ptosis had resolved. Extraocular movements were full and the eyes were well aligned. However, the pupils remained unresponsive to light and accommodation. The mild bitemporal hemianopsia remained unchanged from baseline on automated visual fields.

case_info.explanation: Based on the acute presentation of symptoms and signs starting immediately after surgery and change in the appearance of tumor on MRI (loss of central enhancement), a diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy was made. The ophthalmoplegia in ocular motor apraxia can be overcome with vestibular ocular reflex, which was not the case here. The absence of exophthalmos and normal intraocular pressure argue against the diagnosis of orbital compartment syndrome. Imaging does not support the diagnosis of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pituitary apoplexy is an acute-onset syndrome due to hemorrhaging and/or infarction of the pituitary gland. Postoperative pituitary apoplexy has been reported after cardiac surgery, abdominal surgery, thyroidectomy, laparoscopic lumbar spinal fusion, and knee arthroplasty.1Risk factors proposed during surgery that could lead to pituitary apoplexy include prolonged mechanical ventilation, embolization, unstable blood pressure, anticoagulation, crystalloid hemodilution, previous treatment with dopamine agonists, and radiotherapy.2 Patients with pituitary apoplexy typically present with headaches. Cranial nerve palsies leading to ophthalmoplegia have been reported in about 50% of patients during pituitary apoplexy.1Sixty-four percent of patients can have vision loss from worsening chiasmal compression, which fortunately this patient did not have.3Early neuroimaging study is important to confirm the suspicion of pituitary apoplexy, along with urgent pituitary function tests. Computed tomography scan is often the first study performed in an acute setting and may demonstrate a variably hyperdense mass of the sella and suprasellar region in the presence of hemorrhage. MRI is the preferred study of choice with sensitivity of about 90%.4Appearance of hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy on MRI depends on the sequence and stage of hemorrhage. In the acute phase, hemorrhage is usually hypotense on T2-weighted imaging because of the presence of deoxyhemoglobin, which was not present in the present patient. Infarctive pituitary apoplexy alone, which is a rarer presentation of pituitary apoplexy, has low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and no contrast enhancement of the tumor as seen in this patient. It may have associated rim enhancement.5 Pituitary apoplexy is a vision- and life-threatening neuro-ophthalmic emergency. Before the use of corticosteroids, mortality rates were reported to be as high as 50% because of acute adrenal insufficiency that many of these patients develop. Treatment involves urgent administration of steroids, endocrine evaluation, and urgent surgical intervention for prompt decompression based on severity of presentation. Visual recovery, with or without sequelae, is variable depending on the severity and duration of compression of the optic nerve apparatus. Ophthalmoplegia resolves in the majority of patients, but some patients can have incomplete recovery.6,7 The patient immediately started receiving intravenous corticosteroids under the guidance of endocrinology and neurosurgery. He was monitored for any endocrine deficiencies while inpatient. After no improvement in extraocular movements were noted over 5 days, the patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of pituitary tumor. Pathological evaluation of the tumor confirmed a pituitary adenoma with areas of necrosis consistent with pituitary apoplexy. Postoperative MRI showed successful resection of the large pituitary macroadenoma, with decompression of the optic chiasm. There was some residual tumor in the bilateral cavernous sinuses, basisphenoid, and along the dorsum sella. One year after surgery, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal color vision. Bilateral ptosis had resolved. Extraocular movements were full and the eyes were well aligned. However, the pupils remained unresponsive to light and accommodation. The mild bitemporal hemianopsia remained unchanged from baseline on automated visual fields.

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

A 50-year-old man was referred for ophthalmoplegia that developed immediately after an 8.5-hour robotic cystectomy for small cell cancer of the bladder. After recovering from anesthesia in the postanesthesia care unit, he experienced headache, facial numbness, inability to open both his eyes, and inability to move both eyes in any direction. He had a known enhancing central skull base lesion in sella turcica with compression of the optic chiasm and mild mass effect on the pons that was felt to be a pituitary macroadenoma (Figure). His baseline examination before the cystectomy showed visual acuity of 20/20 OU with intact extraocular movements and unremarkable confrontational fields, although a mild bitemporal hemianopia was seen on automated visual fields. During the bedside examination in the postanesthesia care unit, he was noted to have complete bilateral ptosis. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU with full visual fields on confrontational visual field testing. He had decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve bilaterally. The right and left pupils were 5 mm and 6 mm in size, respectively, in both light and dark. There was no pupillary response to light or accommodation. No exophthalmos was noted. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes. The patient was unable to move either eye in any direction on extraocular motility testing. Vestibulo-ocular reflex did not overcome the ophthalmoplegia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained 12 hours after symptom onset redemonstrating the large sellar mass, which no longer had central enhancement (Figure).

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Based on the acute presentation of symptoms and signs starting immediately after surgery and change in the appearance of tumor on MRI (loss of central enhancement), a diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy was made. The ophthalmoplegia in ocular motor apraxia can be overcome with vestibular ocular reflex, which was not the case here. The absence of exophthalmos and normal intraocular pressure argue against the diagnosis of orbital compartment syndrome. Imaging does not support the diagnosis of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pituitary apoplexy is an acute-onset syndrome due to hemorrhaging and/or infarction of the pituitary gland. Postoperative pituitary apoplexy has been reported after cardiac surgery, abdominal surgery, thyroidectomy, laparoscopic lumbar spinal fusion, and knee arthroplasty.1Risk factors proposed during surgery that could lead to pituitary apoplexy include prolonged mechanical ventilation, embolization, unstable blood pressure, anticoagulation, crystalloid hemodilution, previous treatment with dopamine agonists, and radiotherapy.2 Patients with pituitary apoplexy typically present with headaches. Cranial nerve palsies leading to ophthalmoplegia have been reported in about 50% of patients during pituitary apoplexy.1Sixty-four percent of patients can have vision loss from worsening chiasmal compression, which fortunately this patient did not have.3Early neuroimaging study is important to confirm the suspicion of pituitary apoplexy, along with urgent pituitary function tests. Computed tomography scan is often the first study performed in an acute setting and may demonstrate a variably hyperdense mass of the sella and suprasellar region in the presence of hemorrhage. MRI is the preferred study of choice with sensitivity of about 90%.4Appearance of hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy on MRI depends on the sequence and stage of hemorrhage. In the acute phase, hemorrhage is usually hypotense on T2-weighted imaging because of the presence of deoxyhemoglobin, which was not present in the present patient. Infarctive pituitary apoplexy alone, which is a rarer presentation of pituitary apoplexy, has low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and no contrast enhancement of the tumor as seen in this patient. It may have associated rim enhancement.5 Pituitary apoplexy is a vision- and life-threatening neuro-ophthalmic emergency. Before the use of corticosteroids, mortality rates were reported to be as high as 50% because of acute adrenal insufficiency that many of these patients develop. Treatment involves urgent administration of steroids, endocrine evaluation, and urgent surgical intervention for prompt decompression based on severity of presentation. Visual recovery, with or without sequelae, is variable depending on the severity and duration of compression of the optic nerve apparatus. Ophthalmoplegia resolves in the majority of patients, but some patients can have incomplete recovery.6,7 The patient immediately started receiving intravenous corticosteroids under the guidance of endocrinology and neurosurgery. He was monitored for any endocrine deficiencies while inpatient. After no improvement in extraocular movements were noted over 5 days, the patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of pituitary tumor. Pathological evaluation of the tumor confirmed a pituitary adenoma with areas of necrosis consistent with pituitary apoplexy. Postoperative MRI showed successful resection of the large pituitary macroadenoma, with decompression of the optic chiasm. There was some residual tumor in the bilateral cavernous sinuses, basisphenoid, and along the dorsum sella. One year after surgery, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal color vision. Bilateral ptosis had resolved. Extraocular movements were full and the eyes were well aligned. However, the pupils remained unresponsive to light and accommodation. The mild bitemporal hemianopsia remained unchanged from baseline on automated visual fields.

case_info.explanation: Based on the acute presentation of symptoms and signs starting immediately after surgery and change in the appearance of tumor on MRI (loss of central enhancement), a diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy was made. The ophthalmoplegia in ocular motor apraxia can be overcome with vestibular ocular reflex, which was not the case here. The absence of exophthalmos and normal intraocular pressure argue against the diagnosis of orbital compartment syndrome. Imaging does not support the diagnosis of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pituitary apoplexy is an acute-onset syndrome due to hemorrhaging and/or infarction of the pituitary gland. Postoperative pituitary apoplexy has been reported after cardiac surgery, abdominal surgery, thyroidectomy, laparoscopic lumbar spinal fusion, and knee arthroplasty.1Risk factors proposed during surgery that could lead to pituitary apoplexy include prolonged mechanical ventilation, embolization, unstable blood pressure, anticoagulation, crystalloid hemodilution, previous treatment with dopamine agonists, and radiotherapy.2 Patients with pituitary apoplexy typically present with headaches. Cranial nerve palsies leading to ophthalmoplegia have been reported in about 50% of patients during pituitary apoplexy.1Sixty-four percent of patients can have vision loss from worsening chiasmal compression, which fortunately this patient did not have.3Early neuroimaging study is important to confirm the suspicion of pituitary apoplexy, along with urgent pituitary function tests. Computed tomography scan is often the first study performed in an acute setting and may demonstrate a variably hyperdense mass of the sella and suprasellar region in the presence of hemorrhage. MRI is the preferred study of choice with sensitivity of about 90%.4Appearance of hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy on MRI depends on the sequence and stage of hemorrhage. In the acute phase, hemorrhage is usually hypotense on T2-weighted imaging because of the presence of deoxyhemoglobin, which was not present in the present patient. case_info.explanation: Based on the acute presentation of symptoms and signs starting immediately after surgery and change in the appearance of tumor on MRI (loss of central enhancement), a diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy was made. The ophthalmoplegia in ocular motor apraxia can be overcome with vestibular ocular reflex, which was not the case here. The absence of exophthalmos and normal intraocular pressure argue against the diagnosis of orbital compartment syndrome. Imaging does not support the diagnosis of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pituitary apoplexy is an acute-onset syndrome due to hemorrhaging and/or infarction of the pituitary gland. Postoperative pituitary apoplexy has been reported after cardiac surgery, abdominal surgery, thyroidectomy, laparoscopic lumbar spinal fusion, and knee arthroplasty.1Risk factors proposed during surgery that could lead to pituitary apoplexy include prolonged mechanical ventilation, embolization, unstable blood pressure, anticoagulation, crystalloid hemodilution, previous treatment with dopamine agonists, and radiotherapy.2 Patients with pituitary apoplexy typically present with headaches. Cranial nerve palsies leading to ophthalmoplegia have been reported in about 50% of patients during pituitary apoplexy.1Sixty-four percent of patients can have vision loss from worsening chiasmal compression, which fortunately this patient did not have.3Early neuroimaging study is important to confirm the suspicion of pituitary apoplexy, along with urgent pituitary function tests. Computed tomography scan is often the first study performed in an acute setting and may demonstrate a variably hyperdense mass of the sella and suprasellar region in the presence of hemorrhage. MRI is the preferred study of choice with sensitivity of about 90%.4Appearance of hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy on MRI depends on the sequence and stage of hemorrhage. In the acute phase, hemorrhage is usually hypotense on T2-weighted imaging because of the presence of deoxyhemoglobin, which was not present in the present patient. Infarctive pituitary apoplexy alone, which is a rarer presentation of pituitary apoplexy, has low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and no contrast enhancement of the tumor as seen in this patient. It may have associated rim enhancement.5 Pituitary apoplexy is a vision- and life-threatening neuro-ophthalmic emergency. Before the use of corticosteroids, mortality rates were reported to be as high as 50% because of acute adrenal insufficiency that many of these patients develop. Treatment involves urgent administration of steroids, endocrine evaluation, and urgent surgical intervention for prompt decompression based on severity of presentation. Visual recovery, with or without sequelae, is variable depending on the severity and duration of compression of the optic nerve apparatus. Ophthalmoplegia resolves in the majority of patients, but some patients can have incomplete recovery.6,7 The patient immediately started receiving intravenous corticosteroids under the guidance of endocrinology and neurosurgery. He was monitored for any endocrine deficiencies while inpatient. After no improvement in extraocular movements were noted over 5 days, the patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of pituitary tumor. Pathological evaluation of the tumor confirmed a pituitary adenoma with areas of necrosis consistent with pituitary apoplexy. Postoperative MRI showed successful resection of the large pituitary macroadenoma, with decompression of the optic chiasm. There was some residual tumor in the bilateral cavernous sinuses, basisphenoid, and along the dorsum sella. One year after surgery, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal color vision. Bilateral ptosis had resolved. Extraocular movements were full and the eyes were well aligned. However, the pupils remained unresponsive to light and accommodation. The mild bitemporal hemianopsia remained unchanged from baseline on automated visual fields.

The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Based on the acute presentation of symptoms and signs starting immediately after surgery and change in the appearance of tumor on MRI (loss of central enhancement), a diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy was made. The ophthalmoplegia in ocular motor apraxia can be overcome with vestibular ocular reflex, which was not the case here. The absence of exophthalmos and normal intraocular pressure argue against the diagnosis of orbital compartment syndrome. Imaging does not support the diagnosis of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pituitary apoplexy is an acute-onset syndrome due to hemorrhaging and/or infarction of the pituitary gland. Postoperative pituitary apoplexy has been reported after cardiac surgery, abdominal surgery, thyroidectomy, laparoscopic lumbar spinal fusion, and knee arthroplasty.1Risk factors proposed during surgery that could lead to pituitary apoplexy include prolonged mechanical ventilation, embolization, unstable blood pressure, anticoagulation, crystalloid hemodilution, previous treatment with dopamine agonists, and radiotherapy.2 Patients with pituitary apoplexy typically present with headaches. Cranial nerve palsies leading to ophthalmoplegia have been reported in about 50% of patients during pituitary apoplexy.1Sixty-four percent of patients can have vision loss from worsening chiasmal compression, which fortunately this patient did not have.3Early neuroimaging study is important to confirm the suspicion of pituitary apoplexy, along with urgent pituitary function tests. Computed tomography scan is often the first study performed in an acute setting and may demonstrate a variably hyperdense mass of the sella and suprasellar region in the presence of hemorrhage. MRI is the preferred study of choice with sensitivity of about 90%.4Appearance of hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy on MRI depends on the sequence and stage of hemorrhage. In the acute phase, hemorrhage is usually hypotense on T2-weighted imaging because of the presence of deoxyhemoglobin, which was not present in the present patient. Infarctive pituitary apoplexy alone, which is a rarer presentation of pituitary apoplexy, has low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and no contrast enhancement of the tumor as seen in this patient. It may have associated rim enhancement.5 Pituitary apoplexy is a vision- and life-threatening neuro-ophthalmic emergency. Before the use of corticosteroids, mortality rates were reported to be as high as 50% because of acute adrenal insufficiency that many of these patients develop. Treatment involves urgent administration of steroids, endocrine evaluation, and urgent surgical intervention for prompt decompression based on severity of presentation. Visual recovery, with or without sequelae, is variable depending on the severity and duration of compression of the optic nerve apparatus. Ophthalmoplegia resolves in the majority of patients, but some patients can have incomplete recovery.6,7 The patient immediately started receiving intravenous corticosteroids under the guidance of endocrinology and neurosurgery. He was monitored for any endocrine deficiencies while inpatient. After no improvement in extraocular movements were noted over 5 days, the patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of pituitary tumor. Pathological evaluation of the tumor confirmed a pituitary adenoma with areas of necrosis consistent with pituitary apoplexy. Postoperative MRI showed successful resection of the large pituitary macroadenoma, with decompression of the optic chiasm. There was some residual tumor in the bilateral cavernous sinuses, basisphenoid, and along the dorsum sella. One year after surgery, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal color vision. Bilateral ptosis had resolved. Extraocular movements were full and the eyes were well aligned. However, the pupils remained unresponsive to light and accommodation. The mild bitemporal hemianopsia remained unchanged from baseline on automated visual fields.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 50-year-old man was referred for ophthalmoplegia that developed immediately after an 8.5-hour robotic cystectomy for small cell cancer of the bladder. After recovering from anesthesia in the postanesthesia care unit, he experienced headache, facial numbness, inability to open both his eyes, and inability to move both eyes in any direction. He had a known enhancing central skull base lesion in sella turcica with compression of the optic chiasm and mild mass effect on the pons that was felt to be a pituitary macroadenoma (Figure). His baseline examination before the cystectomy showed visual acuity of 20/20 OU with intact extraocular movements and unremarkable confrontational fields, although a mild bitemporal hemianopia was seen on automated visual fields. During the bedside examination in the postanesthesia care unit, he was noted to have complete bilateral ptosis. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU with full visual fields on confrontational visual field testing. He had decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve bilaterally. The right and left pupils were 5 mm and 6 mm in size, respectively, in both light and dark. There was no pupillary response to light or accommodation. No exophthalmos was noted. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes. The patient was unable to move either eye in any direction on extraocular motility testing. Vestibulo-ocular reflex did not overcome the ophthalmoplegia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained 12 hours after symptom onset redemonstrating the large sellar mass, which no longer had central enhancement (Figure).
